definition: An autonomous agent (an enemy, a boss) can read as having sophisticated, adaptive, near-intelligent movement while actually being built from a library of complete, fully-authored, NON-interruptible linear actions selected one at a time — the appearance of continuous, clever decision-making comes from a brief, natural-looking hesitation exactly at the moments the agent is choosing its next action (a corner, a threshold, a phase change), which reads as 'thinking' rather than as a seam, plus never breaking a chosen action once it starts.
purpose: Achieve a strong illusion of adaptive, intelligent agent behavior using a much simpler underlying structure (a library of complete linear clips plus a decision point) than true continuous procedural motion would require.
visible_effect: An agent's movement looks fluid and reactive moment-to-moment, with a barely-noticeable brief pause or 'calculating' hitch specifically at points where its path could plausibly branch (a corner, a ledge, after a hit), and otherwise no visible seams within any single chosen action.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The presenter's own experience is direct evidence of the illusion's strength: close analysis was needed to realize an agent that FEELS like it runs a 'complex pathfinding algorithm working in tandem across many limbs' is actually simpler than that — 'lots of complex-looking animations to create this clever illusion.' A boss whose actions cannot be interrupted by player damage reads as MORE seamless, not less, because its timing can always happen 'at the pace the game wants it to happen' rather than needing to handle an interruption gracefully.
physical_interpretation: None — a behavior-authoring and AI-illusion technique, not a physical property.
use_cases: an enemy or agent needing to read as adaptive/intelligent on a constrained, grid-like or otherwise limited traversal space, where the finite real set of situations (moving forward, turning a corner, leaping a gap) can each get one polished, complete linear clip
a boss whose attacks should feel authored and precisely-timed rather than reactive, where refusing to let player damage interrupt an in-progress action preserves that timing entirely
non_use_cases: an agent operating in a truly open, unconstrained space where the number of distinct real situations is too large to cover with a finite clip library — the source notes this technique is helped considerably by the enemy's terrain being 'essentially a giant grid', which keeps the situation count small
a player-controlled character or any context where responsiveness to interruption (not merely to a fresh input) is itself a core requirement
interactions: limb_reset_to_canonical_pose_enables_seamless_bespoke_transitions (this same video) — a companion mechanism from the same source: that entry is HOW a transition into a chosen action looks smooth regardless of prior pose; this entry is WHY the higher-level illusion of intelligent decision-making works at all, given that each chosen action is a complete, non-interruptible clip

blend_tree_locomotion_replaces_state_machine (W05, video 42) — a genuinely instructive tension, not a contradiction: that entry argues AWAY from discrete state machines toward continuous blend spaces specifically for smooth PLAYER locomotion control; this entry shows a state-machine-of-complete-clips can still be the RIGHT choice for an autonomous NPC/agent, because a visible decision hitch reads as intentional 'thinking' for an agent in a way it would not for a player's own directly-controlled character

strike_assist_hit_reaction_camera_relative_correction and other runtime-correction entries (W05) — a different family of technique (real-time correction of an already-playing action) that this entry's boss example deliberately avoids, preferring full authored non-interruptible clips instead
cadence_representation: Not represented, and out of scope for the same reason as this video's companion entry: this is a runtime AI/behavior-tree and animation-selection strategy, not an authored clip's own property. `ai/motion.js` could in principle measure whether an AUTHORED clip's own internal motion is continuous and complete (no internal seams), which is a necessary ingredient this technique depends on, but the DECISION-making layer that selects which complete clip to play, and the deliberate non-interruptibility policy, are both runtime/game-logic concerns entirely outside `ai/`'s pure, project-data scope.
control_surface: None — outside this build's scope entirely.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not measurable in this build: no track or measurement represents an agent's decision logic, action-interruptibility policy, or inter-action selection timing.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — outside this build's scope entirely; the individual complete clips this technique depends on are ordinary keyframe authoring.
failure_modes: placing the decision hitch somewhere that does NOT read as a natural pause point (mid-motion rather than at a corner/threshold), breaking the illusion by making the hitch look like a stutter rather than a thought
attempting this approach in a space too open/varied for a finite clip library to cover convincingly, exposing the seams between distinct situations the source's own grid-constrained example avoids
roblox_considerations: Directly reachable via ordinary server-side AI/behavior-tree logic selecting between complete `AnimationTrack`s, refusing to interrupt one once started except at declared decision points — no bespoke engine feature required beyond normal state/behavior-tree game logic.
performance_implications: Likely cheaper to author and run than a true continuous procedural/pathfinding system, which is the source's own implied point in being surprised the result wasn't one.
examples: 'if you watch an EMMI, and I mean really watch an EMMI, everything is all still one action after another... you can see when an EMMI reaches corners and turns and approaches certain thresholds, there's a slight halt where you can see it calculating which animation to perform next' (video @ 25:22–26:12)

the same principle for a boss: 'his actions can't really be interrupted... this is generally what allows them to be quite seamless, because they can happen at the pace the game wants them to happen' (video @ 18:55–19:05)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/1B1beXTnvEI @ 18:55–19:05, 25:22–27:13 — the presenter states this directly as a conclusion reached from close repeated observation, correcting their own initial assumption of a more complex underlying system; transcript-only, no frames extracted this session; experimental until validated
